workload: A base contract arrives with several amendments on top. The values we need depend on reading across sections, on effective dates, and on how far each amendment reaches. We want an evidence-backed comparison against what our business system already holds, with lineage a reviewer can follow, and the runs are long enough that we need to resume after a failure rather than start over.

Every month we get thousand-page payment applications mixing typed, scanned and handwritten pages. Deciding whether the charges are allowable depends on a master agreement, party-specific contracts, and amendments that keep getting added. We want the potentially non-compliant charges plus the contract chain behind each one.

We test a couple of hundred controls against evidence files, mostly spreadsheet exports. A control might need a data transformation, some exact arithmetic, and then a judgement about whether the evidence satisfies policy. Inputs and procedures differ per control, and reruns must produce identical numbers.

Purchase-order exports reach us from dozens of suppliers with no fixed template. Column layouts differ, the header is not always on the first row, and many are not in English. Before we can process rows we need to work out which sheet holds the data, which row is the header, and which columns matter.

An agent reviews invoice and backup attachments on fixed-asset addition requests, a few hundred a month. It does not need to capture a field set — it needs enough of the document content as evidence to recommend approve, reject, or send to a human, and an analyst stays the final approver.

We get a handful of clean single-page letters a day and need three named values off them inside a larger agent task. Nobody has asked for a field accuracy target and there is no correction workflow planned.

We receive thousand-page image-only bundles at high monthly volume. Several named document types are buried somewhere in each one. We need to find them and their page ranges, apply a rule about which copy wins when the same document appears twice, and only then pull fields from what is left.
A bundle contains many documents. The first job is to locate one specific contract inside it. A separate, later job asks whether the buyer actually signed that contract.

Inbound correspondence has to be routed into about seven predefined buckets — authorization, denial, clinical request, pending review and a few more. Sending an authorization down the denial path costs far more than an ordinary mix-up, so we cannot just optimise overall accuracy.

A contract of anywhere from a few dozen to a couple of hundred pages comes in and we need a cited assessment: where does it conflict with our standard terms, and which required provisions are missing entirely? Saying nothing is wrong has to actually mean the whole document was reviewed.

A defined set of a few dozen documents holds the evidence for one written risk assessment. What matters is the synthesis across them — contradictions between sources, and claims we can trace back to the document that supports them. Response time is not the priority.

The evidence for a profile and discussion guide has already been collected. What remains is turning it into a coherent briefing with citations that a human approves, refreshed on a schedule. Gathering, storage and approval are handled elsewhere.
Staff keep asking policy and system-support questions against a standing document collection that we maintain and reuse. A typical question is answered by one procedure or a couple of passages.

Analysts need source-backed lookups of plan language. The applicable plan is known, its indexed version is current, and the provision they want is answerable on its own. The analyst still makes the decision.

Our knowledge base is partitioned by bureau, and the same term means different things in different bureaus. A question asks for a definition or a documented procedure that is answerable inside one known bureau.

A line item has to be interpreted against an item master plus two further attribute sources before it means anything. The identifiers are noisy — aliases, placeholder substitution, seasonal variation — and what we need to look up next depends on what the previous lookup returned.

An incoming request has to be normalized before the receiving office can act. The terminology it should use, the artifacts it should carry and the obligations that apply are scattered across the domain corpus, and the mappings are not all defined up front.

Several thousand controlled documents might be affected by a terminology change and somebody has asked which ones. Finding candidates needs iteration — separating current text from revision history, chasing ambiguous references — but the answer is phrased as a complete list.

Short, consistent forms of a few pages each carry the same fixed fields every time, and they are already separated by type. Releasing an incorrect value is expensive, so review gates, a correction workflow and field-level evaluation are hard requirements.

Forms arrive with handwriting and low-contrast scans, carrying a couple of dozen fields across several groups. Ordered items have to be told apart from reported values and ranges, and a human validates fields before anything is released.

Each document describes fifteen to twenty or more repeated entities, with each entity's fields spread across the document. One file can produce hundreds of output rows across a dozen columns, and results keep coming back silently truncated.

Every shipment record carries an operational notes field with no format, written in a mix of two languages — terse fragments, inline rates, status shorthand. Operators read them next to a per-customer rate table and key charges into billing, tens of thousands of records a month. One note can imply several separate charges.

Invoice line items need a tax category from a set of a few hundred. Only items above a value threshold get reviewed today. We have a taxability matrix, and condensed it is a couple of hundred rows — small enough to sit alongside each line item rather than be looked up.

Each claim line item goes through five separate judgements — diagnosis matching, beneficiary exclusion, policy exclusion, treatment validation, benefit classification. None of them needs another line item. A case is only safe to auto-process if every judgement on every line is right.
We have a table of orders and need a new column holding the number of days between the order date and the ship date, plus a flag for anything over thirty days. Same rule for every row, no exceptions.

Each transaction row carries a warehouse code. We need the warehouse's region and country appended to every row from our warehouse master, which is an exact-key mapping with no ambiguity and no missing codes.
Given a month of already-structured claim records, produce the count and total value grouped by payer and by status, and write the result to a file.
